newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria bans protests to mark annulled election.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria bans protests to mark annulled election.

text.p: Nigerian police said on Wednesday that no demonstrations would be allowed to mark the fourth anniversary on Thursday of the annulled presidential election on June 12, 1993.
Africa's most populous nation has been in crisis since the then ruling generals scrapped the poll, presumed to have been won by detained businessman Moshood Abiola.
But Nigeria leads a West African force trying to restore democracy in Sierra Leone, where soldiers seized power on May 25.
A police statement issued in the federal capital Abuja said no permits had been issued to any group to hold rallies.
"Police area commanders and divisional officers nationwide have been ordered to stop any demonstrations in their areas of jurisdiction," it said.
"The safety of anyone who violates this ban cannot be guaranteed by the police," said Abubakar Tsav, police chief for Lagos state, hotbed of opposition to military rule.
Opposition and pro-government groups had planned rival rallies for June 12 but it was doubtful any would go ahead after the police warning.
Despite heavy rain in Lagos on Wednesday police rolled out armoured vehicles as armed riot police patrolled different parts of the city to dissuade intending protesters.
The state news agency NAN said an armoured personnel carrier had been stationed near the Lagos home of Abiola, who has been detained since June 1994 when he declared himself president.
Nigeria is shunned by the West and several other powerful nations for lack of democracy and alleged human rights abuse.
The current military ruler General Sani Abacha is implementing a programme to hand over power next year but the opposition says his hidden ambition is to transform himself into an elected leader.
The umbrella opposition National Democratic Coalition (NADECO) on Wednesday reiterated its position that it did not intend to mark June 12 with any processions or demonstrations.
"We are not sending out anybody to protest because we know the kind of government we have," Abraham Adesanya, deputy chairman of NADECO said.
But from the United States a Nigerian group faxed a statement to the media in Lagos saying it planned to hold a rally in Boston and to launch an opposition radio.
Nigeria activists said Abacha's transition to democracy programme had not healed the wounds of the annulled poll.

"The first condition for the rebirth of Nigeria on the basis of any politicial programme is the termination of military rule," said the Civil Liberties Organisation in a statement to mark the anniversary of "June 12" as the annulled poll is known.
The Constitutional Rights Project said the only solution was to free all detainees including Abiola to negotiate with him to have a government of national unity.
